# DEVIANT

A cinematic branching-narrative game in the vein of *Detroit: Become Human*, built from scratch in
TypeScript and Three.js. Androids that have begun to feel, the people who own them, and the machine
sent to hunt them down.

**Everything you see is generated by code.** There are no image, model, audio or font assets in this
repository: materials, skies, characters, faces, hair, rain, music, ambience and sound effects are all
synthesised at runtime.

## Running it

```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # http://localhost:5173
```

- `npm run dev` — play it
- `npm run build` — typecheck and bundle
- `npm run preview` — serve the static build on port 4173

Useful URL parameters:

| Parameter | Effect |
|---|---|
| `?demo=1` | Auto-plays the whole story with pre-selected choices |
| `?chapter=ch3` | Starts at a given chapter (`ch1`…`ch5`) |
| `?only=1` | Stops after one chapter |
| `?q=low\|medium\|high\|ultra` | Forces a quality tier |
| `?scene=lookdev` | Material and lighting test bed |
| `?scene=char&who=nova&framing=face` | Character look-development view |
| `?scene=still&chapter=ch1&shot=two` | Static staged frame, for reviewing composition |

## The story

Five chapters, roughly ten minutes of play, across three sets.

1. **PROTOCOL** — an investigator android interrogates a deviant that killed its owner.
2. **HOUSEHOLD** — a domestic android watches a man raise his hand to his daughter.
3. **RUN** — the android and the child, out in the rain, with a bulletin out on them.
4. **PREDATOR** — the investigator reconstructs the scene and decides what to put in his report.
5. **DAWN** — the two of them meet. Three endings, depending on what you chose along the way.

Choices are timed, they set flags, and they gate later options: the third ending in chapter five is
only offered if you withheld evidence in chapter four. A branch flowchart between chapters shows the
paths you took and the ones you missed.

## Architecture

```
src/engine/      renderer, procedural textures, HDR sky and IBL, post-processing, rain, audio
src/characters/  skeleton, SDF body, parametric head, facial rig, animation, the cast
src/world/       environment modules (street, apartment, interrogation room) and props
src/game/        narrative graph, director, cinematic camera
src/ui/          the diegetic interface layer (DOM)
src/dev/         look-development and still-frame harnesses
tools/           headless screenshot and offline video capture
```

### Rendering

An HDR forward pipeline with physically-based lighting. The sky is a procedural shader rendered into a
cube target, used both as the visible background and, through `PMREMGenerator`, as the image-based
lighting environment. Post-processing runs through `postprocessing`:

- ground-truth ambient occlusion, depth of field, mip-mapped bloom, AgX tone mapping, SMAA
- a custom **film grade** pass (lift/gamma/gain, split toning, bleach bypass, optical vignette)
- a custom **atmosphere** pass with world-space exponential height fog integrated along the view ray,
  aerial perspective, and screen-space volumetric light shafts
- a custom **lens rain** pass with refracting droplets and run-off on the front element
- a custom **scan vision** pass for the android analysis mode (depth-edge outlines, sweep, data grid)
- custom **deviancy glitch** and **letterbox** passes

Materials are synthesised procedurally: each generator fills albedo, height, roughness, metalness and
occlusion in one pass, and the normal map is derived from the height channel with a wrapping Sobel
filter so everything tiles seamlessly.

### Characters

Bodies are signed distance fields — a generalised-cylinder torso plus tapered limbs — polygonised with
Surface Nets, so every joint join is organically smooth and normals come from the analytic gradient.
The mesh is then skinned to the rig by proximity weighting, and each triangle is classified as skin,
cloth or shoe from its owning bone plus explicit garment cut-offs, which gives clean hems.

Heads are separate and higher resolution. A lofted skull is sculpted by a stack of soft-falloff
deformers — effectively digital clay brushes — all positioned from anatomical landmarks expressed as
fractions of head height, so one sculpt scales correctly from an adult to a child. On top of that:

- twelve morph targets for expressions and visemes, built from region masks
- per-vertex pigmentation (lips, blush, shadowed sockets, reddened ears, beard shadow), which is what
  stops a face reading as a uniformly-coloured mask
- eyelids as separate spherical shells that rotate around the eyeball, so blinks work without cutting
  an aperture into the mesh
- a dental arch, tongue and dark oral cavity, so an open mouth is not a hole into the skull
- card hair grown in the scalp's spherical parameterisation so it follows the skull instead of
  shooting out along the surface normal
- the android temple LED, which tracks software instability from blue through yellow to red

Skin uses a cheap but convincing subsurface term driven by an explicit key-light direction: back-lit
thin areas glow warm and the diffuse terminator is wrapped so faces never go abruptly black.

Animation is a layered stack: a hand-authored pose library and clips, then procedural breathing and
weight shift, then a look-at that splits rotation between chest, neck, head and eyes with saccades and
blinks, then the face — expression morphs underneath speech visemes generated from the dialogue text.

### Direction

The script is data. A chapter is a graph of nodes, each a list of beats — lines, choices, camera
setups, staging, quick-time events, analysis sequences, music and effect cues. The director performs
them, and shots are described in film terms rather than coordinates:

```ts
line('nova', 'She has a name. Ask me her name.', {
  emotion: 'determined',
  cam: single('nova', 'close', { angle: 20, duration: 1.2, handheld: 0.5 }),
})
```

`CameraDirector` solves those against the actors' live positions, derives two-shot distance from the
lens so both actors actually fit, and clamps solved positions against scene geometry so the camera
never ends up inside a wall. That clamp is cached and revalidated on a timer rather than raycast every
frame — doing it per frame cost more than the entire rest of the frame.

All waiting in the director goes through its own clock, advanced from the stage update. Combined with
an externally-driven UI clock, that makes a performance identical in real-time play and under
fixed-step offline rendering — which is what makes deterministic video capture possible.

## Tooling

Development ran without a GPU, so quality was reviewed by rendering headlessly through Chrome and
SwiftShader:

```bash
node tools/shoot.mjs --shots="still@0.4" --w=960 --h=540 --extra="chapter=ch3&shot=two"
node tools/record.mjs --chapter=ch1 --only=true --fps=20 --w=854 --h=480
```

`record.mjs` steps the game one fixed frame at a time and encodes the result with ffmpeg, so a
rasteriser running at roughly one frame per second still produces correctly-paced video.

## Controls

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| Mouse / arrow keys + Enter | Navigate menus and choices |
| `1`–`4` | Pick a choice directly |
| Space / Enter | Advance dialogue |
| `E`, Space | Quick-time event prompts |
| Escape | Pause |
